title: Yuksom 1642 and the birth of the Namgyal kingdom
meta_description: How three lamas crowned Phuntsog Namgyal at Yuksom in 1642, what the royal chronicle and historians say, and how to walk Norbugang, Kathok Lake and Dubdi.
summary: Sikkim's 333-year Namgyal monarchy began at Yuksom, where tradition says three Tibetan lamas crowned Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal in 1642. The stone seats of Norbugang, Kathok Lake and Dubdi Monastery still stand within a short walk. Here is the story as the royal chronicle tells it, what historians add, and how to walk it.

sections.heading: A village where a kingdom began
paras: Yuksom today is a village of about 2,000 people at 1,780 m in Gyalshing district (West Sikkim), best known as the start of the Goecha La trek. Wikipedia, drawing on the Sikkim government and older histories, records it as the first capital of the Kingdom of Sikkim and the place where the Namgyal dynasty began in 1642. That dynasty ruled, through twelve Chogyals, until 1975, when Sikkim became the 22nd state of India.

The name is usually explained as the meeting place of the three learned monks. Older sources also call the area Norbugang, and the hills around it Ney-Pemathang. You can walk every site connected with the founding in one unhurried day, and they mean far more once you know the story behind them.

Yuksom's importance did not start with the kings. In Sikkimese Buddhist tradition it is one of four sacred places of Demazong, the valley of rice blessed by Guru Padmasambhava, and Wikipedia notes that these four are read as the plexuses of a human body, with Yuksom as the third eye. Tashiding, 19 km away, is another. That older sacred geography explains why the lamas chose this basin above the Rathong Chu for the coronation rather than a larger settlement, and why pilgrims still come here as well as trekkers.

sections.heading: Before 1642: a pact of blood brotherhood
paras: The story starts centuries before Yuksom. Sikkimese migration narratives, summarised in Wikipedia's article on Khye Bumsa, tell of a prince of the Minyak house from Kham in eastern Tibet who settled in the Chumbi Valley. Childless, Khye Bumsa crossed into Sikkim to seek the blessing of Thekong Tek, a Lepcha holy man and chief. Three sons followed, and the two men sealed an alliance at Kabi, north of present-day Gangtok, with stones raised as witnesses and Kangchenjunga invoked.

The site, Kabi Lungchok, still has its standing stones and statues of the two blood brothers. The treaty is remembered as the first bond between the Bhutia (Lho), Lepcha (Mon) and Limbu (Tsong) peoples, the Lho-Mon-Tsong-sum, which later Sikkimese rulers held up as the foundation of the kingdom. Phuntsog Namgyal is described in the royal genealogy as a fifth-generation descendant of Khye Bumsa's line.

sections.heading: Three lamas from three directions
paras: In Sikkimese Buddhist tradition, Guru Padmasambhava, who brought tantric Buddhism to Tibet in the 8th century, hid Sikkim as a beyul, a sacred hidden valley to be opened in a time of need. In the 1640s three lamas of the Nyingma school came to open it. The best known is Lhatsun Namkha Jigme, called Lhatsun Chenpo, who is said to have crossed the high passes from the north. Ngadak Sempa Chenpo came from the west and Kathok Rigzin Chenpo from the south.

They met at Norbugang. The prophecy, as the royal chronicle tells it, called for a fourth man from the east. Messengers went looking and found Phuntsog, then 38, near present-day Gangtok, churning milk. He offered them refreshment and shelter, and the lamas took his hospitality and his royal descent as signs that he was the one. They brought him to Yuksom.

The meeting of the lamas and the man from the east is the moment Sikkimese Buddhists remember, and you will hear versions of it from monks, guides and homestay hosts across the west. Details differ in the telling, which is normal for a story passed on for nearly four centuries.

sections.heading: The coronation at Norbugang
paras: The crowning took place on a stone platform on a pine-covered hill above the village. Phuntsog Namgyal was given the title Chogyal, a king who rules according to the dharma, and anointed with water from a sacred urn. The stone seats known as the Throne of Norbugang still stand under the trees, with a chorten beside them. Kathok Lake, at the edge of the village, carries the name of Kathok Rigzin Chenpo, as told locally, and its water is still used in Sikkimese royal and religious ceremonies.

Wikipedia's Yuksom article records that the new king set up the first central administration, dividing the kingdom into twelve dzongs, or districts, each under a Lepcha dzongpon (governor). In the Chogyal's early decades the realm reached into the Chumbi Valley, parts of what is now Darjeeling district and parts of eastern Nepal. Later wars with Bhutan and the Gorkha kingdom of Nepal cut it back to roughly the present borders.

sections.heading: What the sources say, and where they differ
paras: Most of the story above comes from Sikkim's own royal chronicle, the History of Sikkim compiled in 1908 by the ninth Chogyal, Thutob Namgyal, and Maharani Yeshay Dolma, and from works that followed it, such as H. H. Risley's Gazetteer of Sikhim (1894). They are the voice of the court, and they tell the founding as a single, destined event.

Modern historians read them more carefully. In Opening the Hidden Land: State Formation and the Construction of Sikkimese History (Brill, 2011), Saul Mullard, working from earlier Tibetan and Sikkimese documents, argues that the kingdom took shape more gradually through alliances with local Lepcha and Limbu leaders, and that the neat date of 1642 and some of the lamas' roles were fixed by later writers. Monastery founding dates also vary: Dubdi is traditionally dated to 1701, while Pemayangtse and Tashiding trace their origins to the 1640s. We tell the traditional story because it is how Sikkim remembers its beginning, and we flag these debates so you can read further.

sections.heading: From Yuksom to Rabdentse, Tumlong and Gangtok
paras: Yuksom was the capital for only 28 years. In 1670 the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the court to Rabdentse, on a ridge near today's Pelling. According to Wikipedia's article on him, his Limbu queen named the new palace Song Khim, new house in Limbu, a name that may have given the word Sikkim. Rabdentse was later destroyed by invading Gorkha forces, and the court moved to Tumlong in the north and finally, in 1894, to Gangtok, where the palace still stands.

Through all these moves Yuksom kept its role in ritual. Dubdi Monastery, the retreat, was built on the hill above in the early 18th century and is linked by tradition with Lhatsun Chenpo, and the coronation site remained a place of pilgrimage. The twelfth and last ruling Chogyal, Palden Thondup Namgyal, lost his throne in 1975.

sections.heading: Walking the founding story today
paras: Give the history a full day in Yuksom. Start early for Dubdi, while the path is cool, then come down for lunch and spend the afternoon at Norbugang and Kathok Lake. A local guide from the village, about ₹1,000–1,500 for the day, will point out details you would miss, from the footprint said locally to be Lhatsun Chenpo's on the throne stones to the old prayer walls. Entry to the sites is free or by small donation; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Why is Yuksom important in Sikkim's history?
faqs.a: Yuksom was the first capital of the Kingdom of Sikkim. Tradition holds that three Tibetan lamas crowned Phuntsog Namgyal as the first Chogyal at Norbugang in Yuksom in 1642, starting the Namgyal dynasty that ruled until 1975. The coronation seats, Kathok Lake and Dubdi Monastery still stand within walking distance of the village.

faqs.q: Who crowned the first Chogyal of Sikkim?
faqs.a: According to the royal chronicle, three lamas of the Nyingma school: Lhatsun Namkha Jigme (Lhatsun Chenpo), Ngadak Sempa Chenpo and Kathok Rigzin Chenpo, who are said to have come from the north, west and south. They found Phuntsog Namgyal, the man from the east named in a prophecy, and crowned him at Norbugang in Yuksom.

The name is usually explained as the meeting place of the three learned monks, after the three lamas who gathered there to crown the first Chogyal in 1642. This is the explanation given on Wikipedia and in local tradition. The area was also called Norbugang, and the hills around it Ney-Pemathang.

faqs.q: Can you visit the Norbugang coronation throne?
faqs.a: Yes. The stone seats stand under pine trees about 1 km from Yuksom bazaar, an easy walk, with a chorten beside them. There is no ticket, though a small donation is welcome. Walk clockwise around the chorten, do not climb on the stones and keep voices low, as it is still a place of prayer.

1642 is the traditional date given in the royal History of Sikkim and used by the state today. Historian Saul Mullard, in Opening the Hidden Land (Brill, 2011), argues that the kingdom formed more gradually through alliances with Lepcha and Limbu leaders and that the single date was fixed later. Both views are worth knowing when you stand at Norbugang.

It is the idea of unity between the three founding peoples of Sikkim: the Lho (Bhutia), the Mon (Lepcha) and the Tsong (Limbu). It is traced to the blood-brotherhood pact between Khye Bumsa and the Lepcha chief Thekong Tek at Kabi Lungchok, north of Gangtok, and was later used by the Chogyals as a founding principle.

faqs.q: When did the capital move from Yuksom?
faqs.a: In 1670, when the second Chogyal, Tensung Namgyal, moved the court to Rabdentse near Pelling. Rabdentse was later destroyed by Gorkha forces from Nepal, after which the capital moved to Tumlong in North Sikkim and, in 1894, to Gangtok. The Rabdentse ruins are an Archaeological Survey of India protected site you can walk to from Pelling.

faqs.q: How do I get to Yuksom?
faqs.a: Yuksom is about 35 km and 1.5–2 hours from Pelling, and about 170 km and 6.5–7.5 hours from NJP or Bagdogra via Jorethang, Legship and Tashiding or Gyalshing. Shared jeeps run from Gyalshing and Jorethang, mostly in the morning. Most travellers combine two nights in Pelling with two in Yuksom.

faqs.q: Is there a museum about the Chogyals in Yuksom?
faqs.a: Not a formal one. The founding story is told through the sites themselves: Norbugang, Kathok Lake and Dubdi Monastery. For royal objects, manuscripts and Buddhist art, visit the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology in Gangtok, which holds one of the most important collections in Sikkim. A local guide in Yuksom adds much to the walk.
